inputs.original_text: More than 58 lakh names were deleted from West Bengal’s electoral rolls, yet the tribunals meant to hear challenges are still not operational—even after the Supreme Court directed their creation. The software is ready, but basic arrangements, including where the tribunals will sit, are still being discussed by the state government and Calcutta High Court. When so many people risk losing their vote, delays in setting up a meaningful appeal process are not a minor administrative issue: they leave people, especially those with the least power to navigate bureaucracy, waiting to defend a fundamental right.
inputs.modified_text: More than 58 lakh people have had their names deleted from West Bengal’s electoral rolls, while the promised tribunals to challenge those removals remain unready despite the Supreme Court’s direction. The software exists; the basic question of where hearings will happen is still being discussed. That is not a harmless procedural snag. When people’s right to vote depends on navigating a system that has not even been put in place, the burden falls hardest on those with the least time, money, and access to bureaucratic power. A right without a timely, meaningful appeal is a right the state is failing to protect.
